To be sure, the EPA may foreclose the citizen suit by itself bringing 
suit. This allows public authorities to avoid private enforcement only by 
accepting private direction as to when enforcement should be 
undertaken—^which is no less constitutionally bizarre. Elected officials are 
entirely deprived of their discretion to decide that a given violation should 
not be the object of suit at all, or that the enforcement decision should be 
postponed. * * *
No t e s
1. Mootness. In a part of the opinion not included above, the Court also 
considered whether the plaintiffs claims were rendered moot, either by 
Laidlaw’s compliance with its NPDES permit or its shutdown of the Roebuck 
facility. Just as ripeness doctrine guards against premature litigation, rules of 
“mootness” enable federal courts to avoid deciding cases no longer justifying 
judicial intervention. If, at any stage in a lawsuit, the controversy is no longer 
“Eve,” the court may dismiss. The Supreme Court, however, has characterized 
the doctrine as “flexible,” and courts need not dismiss a controversy as moot if 
the issue presented is “capable of repetition, yet evading review.” Weinstein v. 
Bradford, 423 U.S. 147, 149 (1975).
The Court in Laidlaw reEed on a related principle—that voluntary 
cessation of chaEenged activity is not sufficient to moot a case—to find that the 
issue there was stiE appropriate for judicial review:
The only conceivable basis for a finding of mootness in this case 
is Laidlaw’s volimtary conduct—either its achievement by August 
1992 of substantial compEance with its NPDES permit or its more 
recent shutdown of the Roebuck facEity. It is weE settled that “a 
defendant’s voluntary cessation of a chaEenged practice does not 
deprive a federal court of its power to deternune the legaEty of the 
practice.” “[I]f it did, the courts would be compeEed to leave ‘[t]he 
defendant * * * free to return to his old ways.’ ” In accordance with 
this principle, the standard we have annoimced for determining 
whether a case has been mooted by the defendant’s volimtary conduct 
is stringent: “A case might become moot if subsequent events made it 
absolutely clear that the aEegedly wrongful behavior could not 
reasonably be expected to recur.” The “heavy burden of persua[ding]” 
the court that the chaEenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected 
to start up again lies with the party asserting mootness.
